question: Is China safe for international medical tourists?
answer: Absolutely. China is one of the safest countries in the world for medical travelers. Top hospitals' international departments follow JCI or equivalent international standards, with rigorous safety protocols and dedicated security. Doctors at these departments have extensive experience treating foreign patients, and English-speaking patient coordinators are available to assist you throughout your visit. Major cities like Beijing and Shanghai have modern infrastructure, reliable transportation, and low crime rates — making your medical journey as smooth and safe as possible.

question: Do doctors speak fluent English?
answer: At international departments of top hospitals, yes — core doctors and patient coordinators speak fluent English. Many have trained or conducted research in English-speaking countries. Beyond English, some hospitals also offer Japanese, French, or German language support through dedicated interpreters. For more specialized or rare languages, professional medical translation services can usually be arranged with advance notice. We always recommend confirming language support when booking your appointment.

question: How much can I save compared to the US or UK?
answer: On average, international patients save 40% to 80% on total medical costs compared to the US, and 30% to 60% compared to the UK — including surgery, hospitalization, medications, and follow-up care. For example, a coronary bypass surgery that might cost $100,000+ in the US typically ranges from $15,000 to $30,000 in Beijing at an international department. Savings vary by procedure complexity and hospital tier. Private international hospitals (like United Family) are at the higher end of China's range, while public hospital international departments offer the best value while maintaining excellent quality.

question: What is the typical wait time for surgery?
answer: From initial consultation to surgery scheduling, most procedures can be arranged within 48 hours to 2 weeks — dramatically faster than the months or even years of waiting common in many Western countries. Emergencies are handled immediately. For elective procedures, you can often schedule your surgery before arriving in China by sharing your medical records in advance. This speed is one of the most compelling reasons international patients choose China for their care.

question: Can I use my international health insurance?
answer: Yes, you can use most international health insurance plans in China's top hospitals. However, coverage varies — you should always confirm with your insurer that your plan includes mainland China, and check which hospitals are in their direct-billing network. Most international departments work with major providers like Aetna, Cigna, MSH, Allianz, Bupa, and AIA. With direct billing, you simply present your insurance card and the hospital bills your insurer directly. Without direct billing, you pay upfront and receive detailed bilingual receipts for reimbursement at home.

question: How do I apply for a medical visa to China?
answer: For short initial consultations or evaluations, you may be eligible for visa-free transit (24 hours to 240 hours depending on your nationality and city of entry). For planned longer treatment, you'll typically need an S2 private affairs visa for medical purposes. The process is straightforward: after you confirm your appointment, the hospital international department will issue an official invitation letter. You then submit this letter along with your passport, application form, and other standard documents to the Chinese embassy or consulate in your home country. Processing usually takes 4 to 7 business days. We can help guide you through each step.

question: What if I have an emergency after clinic hours?
answer: All major international departments have 24-hour emergency care, and top-tier hospitals have dedicated emergency green channels for critical cases. In a life-threatening emergency, dial 120 (China's ambulance number) and clearly state 'English service requested' to the dispatcher. Many 120 dispatchers in Beijing and Shanghai speak basic English. For non-life-threatening urgent issues, you can also call the hospital's international patient hotline — most have 24/7 on-call coordinators who can advise and arrange care.

question: Is Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) reliable?
answer: Yes, TCM is a formal, regulated medical system in China with its own research, standards, and evidence base. Tertiary TCM hospitals and the TCM departments of comprehensive hospitals use standardized herbal granules, evidence-based acupuncture protocols, and modern quality control. TCM excels particularly at chronic disease management, pain conditions, post-surgical recovery, fertility support, and overall wellness. It can be used alongside Western medicine in an integrative approach. We recommend trying TCM at established hospitals rather than unregulated clinics to ensure safety and quality.

question: Will my personal medical data be protected?
answer: Absolutely. China has strict medical privacy laws modeled on international standards (similar to HIPAA and GDPR). International departments take special care with foreign patients' medical records, which are stored separately with restricted access. Your data cannot be shared with any third party without your explicit written consent. Hospitals follow rigorous data security protocols, and international patient coordinators are bound by confidentiality agreements. You have the right to access, correct, and request copies of your medical records at any time.

question: What if I need follow-up care after returning home?
answer: International departments understand this need and provide comprehensive bilingual discharge summaries, treatment plans, imaging reports, and pathology results — all in both English and Chinese. You can take these documents to your local doctor at home for continued care coordination. Many hospitals also offer remote follow-up consultations via video call, so you can check in with your treating physician after returning home. If you need medical records translated or additional test results sent after you leave, the international patient office is usually happy to assist via email.
